senses.gloss:
cakṣurdāna
(‘endowing with the eye’)
------------------------------------------
See AKṢIMOCANA.

Cakrapāṇidatta
------------------------------------------
Āyurveda or the science of life has long been accorded a very important status among the various branches of knowledge in हिन्दुइस्म्. It is the first of the four Upavedas or subsidiary वेदस्.
Among the extant works on this science, the two that are considered ancient and highly authoritative are चरक Saṁhitā and सुश्रुत Saṁhitā. The renowned commentaries on these two works—Āyurvedadīpikā or चरक-tātparyadīpikā on the former, and Bhānumatī on the latter—were by one चक्रपाणिदत्त. He lived in the 11th cent. A. D. and was the son of नारायण, an official at the court of the king Nayapāla of Gauḍadeśa. Naradatta was the teacher under whom he was trained.
Among his original works, चिकित्सा-sārasaṅgraha ranks first.
See also CARAKASAṀHITĀ and SUŚRUTASAṀHITĀ.

cākṣuṣī
(‘pertaining to the eye’)
------------------------------------------
The desire to acquire and to use supernatural powers is a natural trait of human beings. It has given rise to a whole range of occult sciences.
One of the powers that is most fascinating and sought after is the clairvoyant power, the power to see at will anything that is taking place anywhere in the world. This is called ‘cākṣuṣī’ in the ancient Sanskrit works. The महाभारत (1.186) refers to it in the episode of अर्जुन and a Gandharva hero Citraratha. अर्जुन taught him about the fire missile (āgneyāstra) and learnt the cākṣuṣīvidyā from him.

Cakrapuṣkariṇī
(‘tank of the discus’)
------------------------------------------
Once विष्णु dug a pit with his चक्र or discus and sat in it performing severe penance. The whole pit was filled with his perspiration. In admiration of this penance शिव shook his head and as a result, his jewelled ear-ornament fell into this pit. Hence it came to be known as ‘Cakrapuṣkariṇī’ or ‘Maṇikarṇikā’. It is the same as the Maṇikarṇikā Ghāṭ of the river गङ्गा in वाराणसी or काशी.

Cakradhara
(‘one who wields the discus’)
------------------------------------------
Cakradhara, who is credited with the forming of the Mahānubhāva Sect of Maharashtra is said to have lived in the 11th cent. A.D. Some aver that the founder was Govinda Prabhu, a great mystic and चक्रधर was only the first apostle. चक्रधर composed a number of sūtras or aphorisms on this cult. This work is known as Sūtrapāṭha among its followers. The sect itself is of the भागवत Cult and bases its teachings mainly on the गीता, the भागवत and the Sūtrapāṭha.
The followers of this sect used to wear dark blue dress, probably in imitation of the colour of Lord Śrī कृष्ण.
Though the movement started in Maharashtra, somehow it did not become very popular. Rather it fell into disrepute due to its neglect of the वेदस् and disregard for the caste and the आश्रम systems. This disrepute made the writers of this sect use esoteric and symbolic language.
Nāgadeva, भास्कर, Keśavarāja Sūri and a few others were its distinguished followers. Nāgadeva is said to have organized the cult on a systematic basis. There were women followers too, some of whom were advanced mystics and poetesses of repute.
In the paurāṇic and hymnal literature the word represents विष्णु/Nārāyaṇa/ कृष्ण since he is the wielder of the discus-weapon (Sudarśanacakra).

cakrapūjā
(‘worship in a circle’)
------------------------------------------
The cult of the देवी or the Divine मोथेर्, though originating from the ऋग्वेद itself (vide 10.125) gradually developed into two main channels: the dakṣiṇamārga or the right-handed path and the vāmamārga or the left-handed path. The latter was perhaps a grotesque metamorphosis brought about by non-Vedic aboriginal and primitive cults. As a result many sex-rites made their way into this left-handed path. The tāntric literature is replete with such rites.
One such abominable rite is the चक्रपूजा or ‘worship in a circle’. According to the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya, an equal number of men and women, without distinction of caste or even blood relationship, secretly meet at night and sit in a circle. The goddess is represented by a यन्त्र or diagram. The women cast their bodices in a receptacle and each of the assembled men finds a female companion for that night by picking up a bodice from the same.
Scholars are of the view that what might have been simple fertility rites of the ancient days, aimed at increasing agricultural production, might have degenerated into such sex-orgies in the name of religion, especially because of the perverted sexual desires of the wealthy and the powerful persons in the society.

cakṣus
(‘the eye’)
------------------------------------------
Eye is the most important of all the sense organs. The sun is described by the वेदस् as the eye of all that exists.
According to the उपनिषद्स् the power to see that exists in the eye, and the power of light capable of revealing objects, that exists in the sun, are both essentially the same; and, आदित्य is the deity that presides over both. When a human being dies, his ‘eye’ (the power to see) gets merged in the आदित्य.
Belief in the evil influence of the eyes of some people (dṛṣṭidoṣa) is common to India as to many other countries. It is said to cause death, illness, injury, poverty and other evil effects. Children and animals are said to be more vulnerable to it. Hence the use of amulets, countercharms and protective gestures has been resorted to over the years. According to the अथर्ववेद, an amulet of the ‘jiṅgiḍa’ plant gives such protection. The same Veda (2.7.5) contains a hymn called ‘Cakṣurmantra’ directed against curses and those who curse, the invoker requesting for the possessor of the ‘evil eye’ to be harmed (so that he will not harm others).
Cakṣu is the name of one of the seven branches of the river गङ्गा after it descended on earth and got divided. It is generally identified with the river Oxus or Amu Darya in central Asia.

cakras
(‘circles or centres’)
------------------------------------------
The शाक्त आगमस्, more commonly known as the तन्त्रस्, declare that the human body is a little universe in itself and that the various tattvas or cosmic principles in च्रेअतिओन् are there embedded in it. However, each of these tattvas has its own centre of activity, the place where it is most preponderant and from where its energies radiate into the system. They have been called ‘cakras’ (circles or centres) and have often been likened to lotuses. They are not anatomical centres like the nerve-plexuses but subtle seats of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, of शक्ति or divine Power.
Works on योग depict fourteen principal nāḍīs or subtle conduits for the flow of prāṇic energy, of which the सुषुम्ना, the iḍā and the पिङ्गला are the most important ones. The सुषुम्ना is situated inside the spinal column and iḍā and पिङ्गला entwine it from left and right. All the three start from the root of the spinal column and end near the centre of the head.
Six चक्रस् are described as being situated in this सुषुम्ना. They are mūlā-dhāra, स्वाधिष्ठान, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddha and ājñā. The seventh, the सहस्रार, is the final destination of the Kuṇḍalinīśakti, the basic power of the human organism which is likened to a coiled serpent lying dormant at the मूलाधार, until it is roused by appropriate yogic exercises.
The mūlādhāracakra is situated in the space between the anus and the generative organ, at the root of the suṣumnānāḍī. It resembles a crimson lotus of four petals. It is the centre of the principle of earth—pṛthvītattva—and controls the sense-organ of smell as also feet, one of the organs of action. ब्रह्मा, along with his शक्ति सावित्री, is the presiding deity of this चक्र.
The svādhiṣṭhānacakra, next in the series, is situated at the root of the genitals and is placed inside the सुषुम्ना. It resembles a lotus of vermillion colour with six petals. It is the centre of the principle of water—the aptattva—and controls the sense organ of taste and also the hands from among the organs of action. विष्णु along with his शक्ति Rākiṇī, is the presiding deity of this centre.
Then comes maṇipūra, at the navel region. It resembles a lotus of dark hue (like the rain clouds) with ten petals. It is the centre of the principle of fire—tejastattva—and controls the sense-organ of sight and the organ of action, the anus. रुद्र with his शक्ति Lākinī is the presiding deity.
The anāhata, situated in the region of the heart, resembles a lotus of twelve petals of blood-red colour. It is the centre of the principle of air—vāyutattva—and controls the sense of touch and the genitals. Īśa with his शक्ति काकिनी, is the presiding deity.
Next comes the विशुद्धचक्र, in the region of the base of the throat. It resembles a lotus of sixteen petals of smoky purple colour. It is the locus of the principle of ether—ākāśatattva—and controls the organ of hearing as also of speech. सदाशिव with his शाकिनी शक्ति is the presiding deity.
Last of this series of चक्रस्, often designated as ‘ṣaṭcakras’, is the आज्ञाचक्र situated in the region corresponding to the middle of the eyebrows. It resembles a lotus of two petals of white colour. It is the centre of the principle of मिन्द्. Śambhu with his शक्ति Hākinī is the presiding deity.
Beyond this there is the सहस्रार-चक्र, resembling a white lotus of a thousand petals, presided over by Parama-शिव himself. It hangs from the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (opening at the top of the skull) and above the सुषुम्ना, head downwards.
In fact all these चक्रस् hang head downwards only, until they are pierced by the कुण्डलिनी, after it is roused from its slumber by appropriate yogic practices. This piercing of the चक्रस् by the कुण्डलिनी is called ‘ṣaṭcakrabheda’. When the कुण्डलिनी reaches the सहस्रार and gets united with Paramaśiva, the योगि will go into समाधि, the superconscious state, experiencing ineffable bliss.
The तन्त्रस् also describe the various results that accrue to a person who contemplates on these चक्रस् in the prescribed manner.
See also KUṆḌALINĪ and TANTRAS.

Cakratīrtha
(‘holy place associated with the discus’)
------------------------------------------
Any holy place, place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, associated with the चक्र or discus of Lord विष्णु, becomes a ‘Cakratīrtha’. The mythological works mention several Cakratīrthas. However, a few of them only, which are more well-known in the modern times, may be mentioned here.
One of the 24 ponds near रामेश्वरम् (in Tamil Nadu) where the pilgrims have their bath, is called ‘Cakra-tīrtha’. The local legend states that the सुदर्शन-चक्र of Lord विष्णु, which was pursuing the sage दुर्वासस् who had offended अम्बरीष, a great devotee of Lord विष्णु, entered into the pond here and disappeared.
There is one चक्रतीर्थ near प्रभास (the modern Somnath, in Gujarat). Lord विष्णु is supposed to have washed his चक्र or discus here after killing all the demons in a battle.
Another चक्रतीर्थ is situated about six miles from Tryambaka near नासिक् in Maharashtra.
Chakdhar in Kashmir considered to be a place of great sanctity, associated with Lord विष्णु, is also known as ‘Cakradhara’ or ‘Cakratīrtha’
The river Tuṅgabhadrā near the ruins of हम्पि (in Bellary district of Karnataka) flows round the Ṛṣyamūka hill and is called चक्रतीर्थ there.

cakraka
(‘[arguing] in a circle’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the defects of लोगिच् while trying to prove a point. For instance, the arguments for and against the existence of God as the intelligent Creator could run something like this:—
Statement:‘This world was created by an intelli-gent agent.’ Objection:‘Since no intelligent creator in this world is seen without a body, then God also must have a body.’ Reply:‘No. You should consider the general sense of intelligent agentship only.’ Objection:‘But this is impossible! Give us an example of an effect that is produced by an intelligent agent who does not have a body.’ Reply:‘For instance, the shoots of corn growing in the field. They have no intelligent human agent behind them.’ Objection:‘Then, how did they grow?’ Reply:‘By God’s agency.’ This is ‘cakraka’ or arguing in a circle since the concept that was sought to be proved viz., God, was itself given as an answer at the end without proving it.

cakravartin
(‘[one whose] wheels of [the chariot] move [unimpeded]’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of an emperor, a sovereign monarch ruling over vast areas and having vassal kings, is not unknown to the ancient Hindu scriptures. The ऐतरेय ब्राह्मण (ch. 39) mentions the names of several emperors such as जनमेजय, Śatānīka and भरत. In the later recor-ded history, several kings have tried to attain the status of emperors. अशोक, Harṣavardhana and समुद्र Gupta are instances to the point.
The word ‘cakravartin’ along with the word ‘samrāṭ’ has commonly been used to denote an emperor. Literally, the word may mean ‘one whose चक्र or wheel of the chariot rotates (vartanam = rotation) unimpeded,’ thereby signifying his absolute conquest over the land. According to the science of Hindu physiognomy, anyone who has the sign of a ‘cakra’ (wheel, discus or lotus) on his hand is a ‘cakravartin,’ and is destined to become an emperor.
Sometimes the word ‘cakra’ is interpreted as ‘maṇḍala’ or circle of kings, चक्रवर्तिन् being their overlord.
A चक्रवर्तिन् is said to possess ‘seven jewels’ (saptaratna). They are: चक्र, chariot, jewel, queen, wealth, horse and elephant. Here ‘cakra’ may mean the auspicious sign of the सुदर्शनचक्र of Lord विष्णु on his hand.
In जैनिस्म्, the word is used as an epithet for a group of twelve great souls like भरत and Brahmadatta. They were emperors in the spiritual field.

cakra
(‘wheel’)
------------------------------------------
The wheel of a chariot is frequently mentioned in the ऋग्वेद as a symbol of the sun. In some of the hymns (vide 1.155.6) the sun is compared to a wheel denoting the principle of time. The कौषीतकि ब्राह्मण (20.1) calls the year as a revolving wheel of the gods, on which they move through all the worlds.
In the Hindu mythological lore, the cakra—translated as ‘discus’—is almost exclusively described as a weapon of war, especially of विष्णु/Kṛṣṇa. It is called ‘Sudarśana’ (‘that with a pleasing appea-rance’) and is shown with six spokes. This confirms the contention of the scholars that it was originally a symbol of the sun and the six spokes represented the six ṛtus or seasons. Sometimes the सुदर्शन-चक्र is shown personified as a minor deity with a hexagon in his background. Brilliant as fire, he has four or eight or sixteen arms holding bow, arrow, trident, noose, goad and other implements as also weapons apart from the usual Vaiṣṇavite symbols. Symbolically, he represents the चोस्मिच् मिन्द्, the will of the Lord to multiply as well as his infinite power to create and destroy the universe. The सुदर्शन-mantra—a special formula pertaining to it—is said to possess the power to neutralize poisons and exorcise malignant spirits.
In the mantraśāstras—sciences dealing with mystic formulae—six ‘cakras’ or arrangements of letters of the alphabet are described which help in determining the suitability of a particular मन्त्र for a particular individual, depending upon his राशि (zodiacal sign) or नक्षत्र (asterism).
In बुद्धिस्म्, the चक्र symbolizes Dharmacakra, the Wheel of Law, its eight spokes representing the eightfold path prescribed by बुद्ध for attaining निर्वाण or emancipation.

cakṣurvrata
(‘vow concerning the eyes’)
------------------------------------------
Keeping the religious vows either for getting a desired fruit or for getting rid of some difficulties, is common to all religions. Such vows in हिन्दुइस्म् are called ‘vratas’.
‘Cakṣurvrata,’ also called ‘netravrata,’ is performed on the second day of the bright half of the month चैत्र (March-April). The performer has to worship the अश्विन्स् (twin deities, said to be the physicians of gods identified with the sun and the मोओन्) and has to subsist only on curds and ghee. It can be done only once or repeated for twelve years. The performer is assured of a good eyesight. If the vow is kept up for twelve years, he will become a king.
